headline: 150-Year-Old Portuguese Cork Company Takes Flight into Space
meta_description: Corticeira Amorim transforms cork into thermal shields for spacecraft and sustainable materials for everything from cruise ships to soccer fields.
summary_short: A Portuguese cork maker with roots stretching back to the monarchy now insulates spacecraft, lines cruise ships, and protects Real Madrid's training fields.
body:
Corticeira Amorim, a 150-year-old company based in Portugal, has quietly revolutionized what cork can do. What began as a traditional bark harvest from cork oak trees has evolved into a sophisticated material science operation producing everything from thermal heat shields for the European Space Agency's IXV re-entry spacecraft to the deck lining of river cruise ships. The company now generates approximately €1 billion in revenue annually and employs 4,000 people across its operations, proving that heritage industries can lead innovation rather than fade away.

At the heart of this transformation lies Herdade Rio Frio, one of the world's largest cork oak plantations located south of Lisbon. Here, the gnarly trees thrive in the Mediterranean climate, each capable of producing harvestable bark for up to 200 years. After reaching maturity at 25 years, a single tree can be harvested nine times, allowing Corticeira Amorim to operate on the long timescales necessary for sustainable forestry. The company's success with aerospace applications for NASA, Boeing, and SpaceX followed its earlier work insulating the IXV spacecraft, opening doors that most traditional material suppliers never imagined.

Beyond space, cork has found surprising earthbound applications. The company developed CorkSorb to absorb crude oil from ocean spills—the cork absorbs only the oil, allowing it to be reused later. Cork pellets, a byproduct of production, now cushion artificial turf fields; research suggests these cork-filled fields experience 40 percent fewer injuries than those using shredded rubber. Real Madrid uses Corticeira Amorim's cork on its training grounds. Meanwhile, at processing plants like Mozelos near Porto, workers continue their ancestral craft much as before, their hands shaping bark into the building blocks of tomorrow's technologies.
quick_facts: Corticeira Amorim: 150-year-old Portuguese cork company now worth €1 billion annually
Cork oak trees produce harvestable bark for up to 200 years after planting
Cork insulates European Space Agency's IXV re-entry spacecraft and NASA missions
Cork-turf fields show 40% fewer injuries than shredded rubber alternatives
Real Madrid trains on Corticeira Amorim cork at their facility
